category.name: People & Identity
category.description: Tools that resolve identifiers — usernames, email addresses, phone numbers — to accounts and online presence. This is the most legally and ethically hazardous category in the catalogue: almost everything here processes personal data about identifiable people, and several entries are lawful in some jurisdictions and not in others. Read the legal notes before, not after.

tools.name: Sherlock
tools.summary: Open-source command-line tool that checks whether a username exists across hundreds of websites.
tools.description:
Sherlock takes a username and tests it against a maintained list of several hundred sites, reporting where a profile with that handle appears to exist. It works by requesting the site's profile URL pattern and interpreting the response.

It is the standard first move when an investigation starts from a handle rather than a name. A handle reused across platforms often links a professional identity to a personal one, or a current account to an abandoned one that is less carefully curated. The abandoned account is usually where the useful material is.

The failure modes matter more than the tool. A hit means 'a profile with this string exists on this site', not 'your subject has an account there' — common handles collide constantly, and some sites return success for any input. A miss means 'this check did not find one', which is not the same as absence: sites change their response patterns, rate-limit the scanner, or require login. Every positive needs manual confirmation by opening the profile and checking it is actually the same person.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, MIT licensed. No account or API key required for the core function.
tools.legalNotes: Sherlock sends real requests to each site, so it is active, not passive — the checks appear in those sites' logs and can trigger rate limiting or blocking of your IP. Automated probing of profile endpoints is contrary to the terms of service of several of the sites checked. The resulting list is personal data about an identifiable person; compiling it needs a lawful basis, and in the EU/UK a documented legitimate-interest or journalistic basis. Using this tool to build a picture of a private individual for personal reasons is not a legitimate purpose and may constitute stalking or harassment under the law of most jurisdictions.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Widely used and actively maintained — a 0.16.x release line was current as of late 2025 — but false positives and false negatives are both routine as sites change. Site coverage drifts constantly. Treat output strictly as a list of leads to verify by hand; never publish or act on an unverified Sherlock hit.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as actively maintained with a current release; the repository itself was not fetched directly, and the exact site count changes with every release.

tools.name: Maigret
tools.summary: Username search across thousands of sites that also extracts profile details and cross-links identifiers.
tools.description:
Maigret began as a fork of Sherlock and went considerably further. It checks a username against a much larger site list — several thousand by default — and, where a profile is found, parses the page to extract details such as display name, bio, location, linked accounts and unique numeric IDs.

That extraction is what makes it more powerful and more dangerous. A numeric user ID recovered from one platform can sometimes be matched on another; a bio field can reveal a real name or an employer that the handle alone would not. Maigret produces HTML and PDF reports, which is convenient for casework and also means a very detailed personal profile now exists as a file you are responsible for.

The same verification discipline as Sherlock applies, doubled: more sites means more collisions, and automated parsing of profile pages misattributes fields regularly.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source. No account required.
tools.legalNotes: Actively requests thousands of endpoints, which is a substantial automated footprint and breaches the terms of service of many of the sites checked. The generated report is a dossier on an identifiable person: under GDPR you become the controller of it the moment it is written to disk, with obligations on lawful basis, minimisation, security and retention. This platform will never store such a profile for you — if you generate one, it lives in your own custody and you should delete it when the investigation ends. Compiling this material about a private individual without a genuine investigative purpose is likely unlawful in most jurisdictions.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Broader coverage than Sherlock and correspondingly noisier. Parsed profile fields are frequently misattributed, and the very large site list includes many low-quality or defunct services that produce spurious hits. Nothing from Maigret should reach a finding without independent manual confirmation.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as an actively used tool with a large site list. The repository was not fetched directly and the default site count varies by release.

tools.name: WhatsMyName
tools.summary: Community-maintained dataset and web interface for username enumeration across hundreds of sites.
tools.description:
WhatsMyName is primarily a curated JSON dataset describing how to test for a username on each of several hundred sites — the URL pattern, the string that indicates a hit, and the expected response code. That dataset is what several other tools consume, which makes it quietly one of the more important pieces of infrastructure in this space.

There is also a hosted web interface, so an investigator can run a check without installing anything. That convenience has a cost: the query runs from someone else's infrastructure and you are trusting the operator with your search terms.

Because the dataset is community-curated with an explicit detection string per site, its false-positive rate is generally better than tools that infer success from status codes alone. It still needs manual confirmation.
tools.costNotes: Free. The dataset is openly published; the hosted interface is free to use without an account.
tools.legalNotes: The same active-probing and personal-data considerations as Sherlock apply. Additionally, when using the hosted web interface rather than running the dataset locally, your query — the subject's handle — is disclosed to the site operator and its infrastructure. For a sensitive subject, run it locally instead.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The curated per-site detection strings make it more precise than status-code-only checkers, and the dataset is actively maintained by the community. Still subject to handle collisions and to sites silently changing behaviour. Confirm every hit manually.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as an actively community-maintained dataset covering several hundred sites. Not fetched directly; the hosted interface's availability was not separately confirmed.

tools.name: holehe
tools.summary: Checks which of a hundred-plus platforms have an account registered to a given email address.
tools.description:
holehe takes an email address and determines which online services have an account associated with it, by exercising each service's registration or password-recovery flow and reading the difference between 'this address is known' and 'this address is not'.

Used carefully it answers a genuinely useful question — where does this address exist? — and it is often how an investigation moves from an address to a set of platforms worth examining.

The mechanism is also the problem, and it deserves to be stated bluntly. Probing password-recovery endpoints can cause the target service to send an email to the address you are testing. That means running holehe against a person's address can notify that person that someone is looking for them. In an investigation where the subject must not know, this can end the investigation, and in a safeguarding context it can put someone in danger.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source. No account required.
tools.legalNotes: This tool can alert the subject. Some modules interact with password-reset functionality, which may cause a notification email to be delivered to the address under investigation. Treat every run as potentially disclosing. Beyond that, deliberately exercising authentication and recovery flows on services you have no relationship with is contrary to the terms of service of most of them, and depending on jurisdiction and framing may be characterised as unauthorised interaction with a computer system. Use it only where you have a defensible investigative purpose and have accepted the notification risk.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Effective when its modules are current, but services change their registration and recovery responses frequently, so modules break quietly and produce false negatives. A negative result is close to meaningless without knowing whether that module still works. Positives are more trustworthy but should still be corroborated.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as a current, widely used tool checking on the order of a hundred-plus platforms. Repository not fetched directly; module health varies continuously.

tools.name: Epieos
tools.summary: Hosted reverse lookup that maps an email address or phone number to associated online accounts and public profile data.
tools.description:
Epieos runs an email address or phone number against a set of platform checks and returns which services recognise it, together with whatever public profile fragments those services expose — a Google account's public name and photo, for instance, or the presence of an account on common SaaS platforms.

It is popular because it is fast, requires no installation, and produces a clean summary that is easy to include in casework. For a due-diligence analyst who needs to know whether a contact address corresponds to a real, aged online identity, it is a reasonable first check.

Because it is hosted, the operator sees every address you look up. For sensitive subjects that is a meaningful disclosure, and a self-hosted alternative should be preferred.
tools.costNotes: Operates on a freemium model: a free account returns limited results from a subset of modules, with output constrained and watermarked, and paid subscription tiers unlock further modules and higher request allowances. Specific prices reported by third parties were not confirmed against the vendor's own pricing page during this review — the pricing page returned an HTTP 403 to automated fetching — so no figure is quoted here.
tools.legalNotes: Every lookup discloses your subject's identifier to a third-party commercial operator, which logs it. The results are personal data and you become their controller once you record them. Some checks Epieos performs are of the same account-existence-probing family as holehe and may in principle be observable by the target platform. Using this to research a private individual outside a legitimate investigative, journalistic or compliance purpose is likely to breach data-protection law and may constitute harassment.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Generally accurate on the platforms it covers and pleasant to use, but coverage is narrower than it appears and results degrade as platforms change their public exposure. A negative result is weak evidence. Free-tier output is truncated, which can create a misleading impression of thoroughness.
tools.confidenceNotes: The service is real and current, but its pricing page could not be fetched during this review (HTTP 403), so all cost detail here is derived from secondary sources and the specific tier structure and prices are unconfirmed.

tools.name: Hunter.io
tools.summary: Finds and verifies professional email addresses associated with a company domain.
tools.description:
Hunter indexes professional email addresses it has observed on the public web and infers an organisation's address format — first.last@, finitial.last@ and so on. Given a domain it returns known addresses and a confidence score; given a name and domain it proposes the likely address.

For corporate investigation and due diligence this is a legitimate and common tool: establishing who works at an entity, and confirming that a contact address in a document matches the organisation's real format, is basic verification work. It is also, plainly, a sales-prospecting product, which shapes its data.

The important limit is that a substantial share of what it returns is generated from a pattern rather than observed. A 'confidence score' on an address that nobody has ever seen used is an estimate, not evidence.
tools.costNotes: A free registered tier provides a small monthly allowance of searches and verifications; paid subscription tiers scale the allowance and add API access and bulk features. Exact current allowances and prices were not confirmed in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Business contact data is still personal data under GDPR when it identifies a natural person, and Hunter's own compliance position rests on legitimate interest for business communication — that basis does not automatically transfer to your investigative use, and you must be able to justify your own processing. Some jurisdictions treat compiled contact lists more restrictively than others. Do not use pattern-guessed addresses to contact people and represent them as verified.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Reliable at identifying an organisation's address pattern; much less reliable at asserting that a specific individual holds a specific address. Distinguish carefully between addresses Hunter says it has observed on a public source (checkable — follow the cited source) and addresses it has generated. Stale entries for departed staff are common.
tools.confidenceNotes: The service is long-established and unambiguously current, but the free-tier allowance and paid pricing have changed repeatedly and were not verified against the primary pricing page in this review.

tools.name: Have I Been Pwned
tools.summary: Tells you which known data breaches an email address or phone number appears in — without exposing any credentials.
tools.description:
Have I Been Pwned, run by Troy Hunt, aggregates the metadata of publicly known data breaches and lets anyone check whether an address appears in one. It reports which breach and what categories of data that breach contained. It deliberately does not return passwords or other credential material.

For an investigator the useful output is not the security warning but the timeline: knowing that an address appeared in a service's 2016 breach establishes that the address existed and was registered with that service by that date. That is a corroborating datapoint for the age and use of an identity, obtainable without touching any stolen credential.

The design restraint is the point, and it is why this entry is here while credential-dump search services are not. HIBP publishes the fact of exposure, not the exposed material.
tools.costNotes: Individual searches through the website are free. The breach-search API is a paid subscription with tiered rate limits, and domain-wide monitoring for a domain you can prove you control is offered on its own terms. As checked, the service reported roughly 17.8 billion compromised accounts across 1,032 breached websites.
tools.legalNotes: Searching HIBP is lawful and does not expose credential material. Note that a result is a statement that an address appeared in a dataset attributed to a breach — publishing 'X was in the Y breach' about a named private individual is a disclosure about that person and needs the same justification as any other. This platform catalogues HIBP precisely because it does not serve credentials; we do not and will not catalogue services that provide plaintext credential search, and using such services can itself be an offence regardless of how the data was obtained.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The most carefully operated resource of its kind. Breaches are verified before loading, sources are documented, and the operator is explicit about uncertainty when a dataset's provenance is unclear. Coverage is limited to breaches that became public and were loaded — absence from HIBP proves nothing about whether an address was ever exposed.
tools.confidenceNotes: Homepage fetched during this review; live, with the account and breach-site counts above read from the page. API pricing tiers were not read from the primary pricing page.

tools.name: Intelligence X
tools.summary: Search engine over archived web, darknet, document and leak-adjacent material, with historical snapshots.
tools.description:
Intelligence X maintains its own archive of material — web pages, paste sites, Tor hidden services, document collections, WHOIS history and data from public leaks — and makes it searchable by selector: email, domain, IP, Bitcoin address, phone number and others. It keeps historical snapshots, so content removed from the live web often remains findable.

Its appeal to investigators is reach into corners other search engines do not index, particularly paste sites and onion services, and its ability to search by structured selector rather than keyword.

It sits in genuinely uncomfortable territory. Some of what it indexes originates from data breaches, and while search results are typically presented as previews with fuller access behind paid tiers, an investigator using it should be clear-eyed that they may be handling material of unlawful origin. That has consequences in some jurisdictions independent of the investigator's intent.
tools.costNotes: A free tier exists and is heavily limited — commonly described as returning only a small number of results per search. Paid individual, professional, API and enterprise tiers are offered at substantially different price points. Prices circulating on third-party comparison sites were not confirmed against the vendor's own pricing page in this review and are therefore not quoted.
tools.legalNotes: Handle with care. Portions of the corpus derive from data breaches. In several jurisdictions, knowingly possessing or further disclosing material obtained through unauthorised access carries liability regardless of who originally obtained it, and a journalistic public-interest defence is jurisdiction-specific and not universal. Downloading and retaining leak-derived personal data makes you the controller of it. Establish your legal footing — ideally with counsel — before using leak-derived results in published work. Searching Tor-indexed content also has its own operational-security implications for the investigator.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Coverage is genuinely distinctive and the historical snapshots are valuable. Provenance labelling is inconsistent, and it is often hard to establish where a given item actually came from or whether it has been altered — which is exactly what you need to know before relying on it. Anything found here needs independent corroboration before it supports a published claim.
tools.confidenceNotes: The service is real and operating, and the existence of a limited free tier is well attested. Current tier structure, prices and the precise composition of the corpus are unconfirmed from primary sources, and the operator's jurisdiction of establishment should be re-checked before any legal reliance is placed on it.

tools.name: Pipl
tools.summary: Commercial identity-resolution service for fraud prevention and KYC; no longer a public people-search engine.
tools.description:
Pipl was for years the default free people-search engine in OSINT training material. That is no longer what it is, and the catalogue records it mainly so that investigators working from older guides understand why the tool they were told to use does not work.

Pipl discontinued its free public search in June 2019 and repositioned as an enterprise identity-resolution and fraud-prevention platform sold to businesses for KYC, trust-and-safety and investigations. Access is through a sales process, with contract pricing and API-based integration.

If you have institutional access it remains a substantial identity-resolution dataset. If you do not, the honest advice is that there is no free Pipl and the many sites offering 'Pipl search free' are unrelated products.
tools.costNotes: Enterprise contracts only, arranged through sales; no free tier and no public self-service signup since the June 2019 discontinuation of free search. Contract values and per-query rates reported by third-party procurement data sources vary very widely and were not confirmed with the vendor in this review, so no figure is quoted.
tools.legalNotes: This is a commercial identity-resolution database built from aggregated personal data, which is a regulated activity in several jurisdictions. In the United States, use for certain permissible purposes may bring it within the Fair Credit Reporting Act — a determination that depends on your use case and that only counsel should make. In the EU/UK, querying it processes special categories of risk-bearing personal data and the customer, not Pipl, bears responsibility for the lawful basis. Contractual terms typically restrict onward disclosure of results.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Data depth is real but the aggregation model produces confident-looking merges of records belonging to different people with similar identifiers — a well-known and serious failure mode for this whole product class. Never treat an aggregated identity record as an identification without independent corroboration from primary sources.
tools.confidenceNotes: The June 2019 discontinuation of free public search and the pivot to enterprise identity verification were confirmed during this review. Pricing is explicitly not verified and deliberately not quantified.

tools.name: PimEyes
tools.summary: Commercial face-search engine indexing faces scraped from the public web. Catalogued as a hazard, not a recommendation.
tools.description:
PimEyes lets a user upload a photograph of a face and returns other images from across the public web that it assesses as containing the same face. It is included in this catalogue because investigators will encounter it and must understand what it is; it is not endorsed, and this platform will never implement or integrate face matching.

What it does is technically effective and that is precisely the problem. Anyone with a photograph can attempt to locate other appearances of that person online. In the hands of a stalker, an abusive ex-partner or a hostile state that is a weapon, and the well-documented pattern of harm is not hypothetical.

The legal position is unsettled and adverse. A German data protection authority concluded in November 2025 that PimEyes' processing of biometric data may be unlawful under the GDPR, while declining to enforce on the basis that the company is established outside its reach; that non-enforcement decision is itself now the subject of litigation brought by the privacy group noyb in April 2026. Poland's data protection authority fined the company in 2022. Separately, the EU AI Act's prohibited-practices provisions became enforceable in February 2025 and include a prohibition on the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build facial-recognition databases.
tools.costNotes: A search can be run without payment but results are obscured; viewing result sources requires a paid subscription, sold in tiers, with additional pricing for alerting and for its takedown-assistance product. Specific current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: This is the most legally fraught entry in the catalogue. Facial images processed for identification are biometric data and special-category personal data under GDPR Article 9, for which the ordinary legitimate-interest basis is unavailable. A German supervisory authority found in November 2025 that the processing may be unlawful under GDPR but declined to act, citing the company's establishment in Dubai and non-responsiveness; noyb filed suit against that authority in April 2026. Poland's DPA imposed a fine in 2022. The EU AI Act, whose prohibited-practices article became applicable in February 2025, bans untargeted scraping of facial images to build face-recognition databases. US state biometric statutes — notably Illinois BIPA and Texas CUBI — create separate and substantial exposure. Uploading a third party's face to this service is itself an act of processing for which you, the uploader, may bear responsibility. Several newsrooms and NGOs prohibit its use outright. Do not use it on a private individual.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Face matching returns similarity, not identity. False positives on people who merely resemble the subject are routine, and the consequences of acting on one are severe and irreversible for the misidentified person. Results are also skewed by whatever the index happens to have scraped, so a null result means nothing. Nothing from this tool should ever stand as an identification.
tools.confidenceNotes: The regulatory history summarised above — the November 2025 Hamburg DPA finding and non-enforcement decision, the April 2026 noyb lawsuit against that authority, the 2022 Polish fine, and the February 2025 applicability of the EU AI Act prohibited-practices provisions — was checked during this review. The company's stated place of establishment is reported as Dubai; treat the jurisdiction field as reported rather than legally determined. Pricing is not verified.
